summary: Extends the SIP REFER method so one request can point at many targets at once. It lets the Refer-To header carry a pointer to a list of URIs and adds the "multiple-refer" option-tag. This is a Proposed Standard, later updated by RFC 8262.

eli5.summary: Suppose you tell a friend to go call five people for you. Instead of five separate notes, you hand over one note that points to a list of everyone to call.

questions: how to refer to multiple resources in sip
what is the multiple-refer option tag
how to refer to multiple targets in sip
subtitle: One SIP REFER request that points at a whole list of targets, so a server can contact them all for you.

tldr.problem: The SIP REFER method asks one user agent to send a request to a single third party. Applications such as conferencing need a server to send requests, like BYE or INVITE, to a whole group.
tldr.mechanism: The REFER carries a URI list in a body part. The Refer-To header points at that body part, and the "multiple-refer" option-tag in the Require header marks the request. The recipient sends one request per list entry.
tldr.outcome: A moderator can remove or invite many participants with one REFER. The implicit subscription is suppressed, so results are learned by other means such as the conference state event package. RFC 8262 updates this RFC.

today: RFC 5368 is a Proposed Standard and is updated by RFC 8262. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Why REFER Needed Multiple Targets
sections.content:
RFC 3515 gave SIP a REFER method. It lets a user agent (UA) ask a second UA to send a SIP request to a third party. For example, Alice, in a call with Bob, can tell Bob's UA to contact Carol, and Bob's UA then sends an INVITE to Carol.

Some applications need a UA to start transactions towards a whole set of destinations. The RFC gives two examples: a conference moderator who wants the conference server to send BYE requests to a group of participants, or to INVITE a set of new participants.

RFC 5368 extends REFER so that one request can refer to many destinations. It also relies on the suppression of REFER's implicit subscription from RFC 4488.
sections.eli5: Normally you can ask a friend to call one person. This RFC lets you ask your friend to call a whole list of people in one go.

sections.title: The Roles: Issuer, Recipient and Target
sections.content:
The RFC reuses the SIP terms UA, UAC and UAS from RFC 3261 and defines three new roles.

  • REFER-Issuer: a user agent issuing a REFER request.
  • REFER-Recipient: the entity that receives the REFER and forwards a SIP request to a number of REFER-Targets. It is typically a network entity, such as a URI-list server, that acts as a UAS for REFER requests and as a UAC for other SIP requests.
  • REFER-Target: a UA of the intended final recipient of a request generated by the REFER-Recipient.

This is an application of URI-list services from RFC 5363: the REFER-Recipient is a URI-list service that invokes the requested SIP method towards each target in the list.
sections.eli5: There are three players. The asker writes the list, the helper reads it, and the people on the list are the ones who get the calls.

sections.title: How a Multiple REFER Works
sections.content:
The REFER-Issuer builds a normal REFER request but puts the targets in a URI list, in the format of RFC 4826, inside a body part. The Refer-To header field holds a pointer to that body part, and the Require header field carries the multiple-refer option-tag.

When the REFER-Recipient receives the request, it creates a new request per REFER-Target and sends one to each. It acts as if it had received a regular REFER for each URI in the list, following the rules of RFC 3515.

The RFC does not give the issuer a way to learn the results for the individual targets. How the issuer is kept informed is service specific. For a conference invitation, the issuer can subscribe to the conference state event package defined in RFC 4575.
sections.eli5: You write one note that points to a list of names. The helper reads the list and sends a separate message to each name.

sections.title: The Option-Tag and the Missing Subscription
sections.content:
The RFC defines a new SIP option-tag, multiple-refer, for the Require and Supported header fields. A UA that lists it in Supported indicates compliance with this specification. A UA that generates a REFER with a pointer to a URI list in Refer-To MUST include it in the Require header field.

A REFER with a single target creates an implicit subscription to the refer event, and NOTIFY requests report the result. With many targets there is no extension that reports the status of several transactions over that subscription. So the issuer SHOULD include the norefersub option-tag in Require and a Refer-Sub header field set to false, both from RFC 4488. The recipient SHOULD honor this and also put Refer-Sub: false in its 200 (OK) response.

RFC 4488 allows a Refer-Sub header only when the issuer is sure the REFER will not fork. The example in the RFC uses a GRUU as the Request-URI for that reason.
sections.eli5: You put a sticker on the note that says it is a list note. You also say you do not need a reply for each person, because you will find out another way.

sections.title: The URI List and the REFER Request
sections.content:
The default format for the list is the resource list document of RFC 4826, extended with RFC 5364. REFER-Recipients MUST support both, and either side MAY support other formats. The body uses the disposition type recipient-list.

The Refer-To header MUST contain a Content-ID URL (RFC 2392) that points to the body part carrying the list. The issuer SHOULD NOT list any URI more than once. RFC 4826 offers hierarchical lists and entries by reference to the XCAP root URI, which this service does not need, so issuers SHOULD use flat lists and SHOULD NOT use entry-ref elements.

With RFC 5364, each URI can carry a copyControl attribute of to, cc or bcc, saying in which role the target gets the request. This makes no sense for mid-dialog requests such as BYE. A URI can also carry the anonymize attribute, which stops the recipient from disclosing that target URI in a list.
sections.eli5: The list is a simple sheet of names. Each name can say whether the person is a main guest or just copied in, and some names can be kept secret from the others.

sections.title: What the REFER-Recipient Does
sections.content:
The recipient follows Section 2.4.2 of RFC 3515 to choose the response status code. It SHOULD NOT create an implicit subscription, and SHOULD add Refer-Sub: false to the 200 OK.

If the list has entries tagged to or cc, and the request suits the service (it is not received mid-dialog, for instance), the recipient SHOULD include a URI list in each outgoing request. In that case it MUST add a Content-Disposition header with the value recipient-list-history and a handling parameter set to optional. It MUST follow RFC 4826 for the anonymize, count and copyControl attributes.

To avoid duplicate requests to the same target, the recipient MUST take into account the actions that Section 4 of RFC 5363 specifies for duplicated URIs. A recipient that receives a list with more information than the RFC describes MAY discard the extra information.
sections.eli5: The helper sends one message per name, tells each person who else was on the list when that is allowed, and makes sure nobody is contacted twice.

sections.title: Example: Removing Conference Participants
sections.content:
In the RFC's example, Carol is the REFER-Issuer and the conference focus is the REFER-Recipient. Carol sends a REFER whose Require header carries multiple-refer and norefersub, whose Refer-Sub is false, and whose Request-URI is a GRUU so the request cannot fork. The body lists three entries, each with ?method=BYE in its URI.

The focus answers Carol with 202 Accepted, then sends a BYE to each of the three targets, Bill, Joe and Ted, and receives a 200 OK from each. The use of REFER to remove participants from a conference is detailed in RFC 4579.
sections.eli5: A meeting leader hands the organizer a list of three people to send home. The organizer tells each of them to leave, and each one says okay.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
A recipient that accepts multiple-target REFERs acts as a URI-list service, so it MUST follow the security rules of RFC 5363. Those rules include opt-in lists and mandatory authentication and authorization of clients.

Recipients SHOULD only accept REFER requests inside an application they understand, such as a conferencing application, and MUST NOT accept REFER requests for methods they do not understand. The aim is that a recipient is never a dumb server whose only job is to fan out random messages it does not understand.
sections.eli5: The helper only works for people it knows, and only on jobs it understands, so nobody can trick it into spamming a whole list.

data.title: Resource list document
data.code:
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<resource-lists xmlns="urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:resource-lists"
           xmlns:cp="urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:copycontrol">
  <list>
    <entry uri="sip:bill@example.com" cp:copyControl="to"  />
    <entry uri="sip:joe@example.org" cp:copyControl="cc" />
    <entry uri="sip:ted@example.net" cp:copyControl="bcc" />
  </list>
</resource-lists>
